name: Whaling at Bering Strait
summary: Communities around Bering Strait hunted whales alongside seals and walrus; gray whale skulls at Chukchi Peninsula sites date between 180 BCE and 560 CE.
description: A 2025 review of Arctic whaling archaeology reports strong evidence that whaling was already an established subsistence strategy in the Okvik and Old Bering Sea cultures on the Chukchi Peninsula coast and the Bering Strait islands, alongside sealing and walrus hunting, though elsewhere it describes Old Bering Sea whaling as occasional; whaling grew in the Punuk period and was the cornerstone of the Thule economy. Numerous gray whale skulls come from sites at Ekven and Uelen dated 180 BCE to 560 CE. An older case, the Old Whaling culture at Cape Krusenstern, Alaska (1200–800 BCE), rests on a bowhead whale skull and large weapon heads, and some archaeologists doubt it because the cultures that followed there show no whale hunting.

impact.note: Whaling reorganised hunting, boat crews and settlement for Bering Strait societies and was carried east by the Thule, but it stayed one part of a mixed economy in one thinly peopled region.

date.label: 1200–800 BCE (disputed)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Radiocarbon dating places the people of the Old Whaling culture at Cape Krusenstern, Alaska, between 1200 and 800 BCE; the same review reports that some archaeologists doubt they hunted whales.

evidence.supports: Radiocarbon dating indicates that these early whalers lived during the period 1200–800 BCE
evidence.locator: Section 2, A brief history of whaling in the Arctic prehistory

date.label: 180 BCE–560 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Numerous gray whale skulls have been found at archaeological sites at Ekven and Uelen on the Chukchi Peninsula, dated 180 BCE–560 CE.

evidence.supports: Numerous gray whale skulls have been discovered at several archaeological sites in Ekven and Uelen on the Chukchi Peninsula (180 BCE–560 CE)
evidence.locator: Section 4, discussion of Mason and Barber

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The card rests on one 2025 review whose chronology is not always consistent; the works it cites (Darwent and Darwent 2016 on Old Whaling; Mason and Barber 2003 on Ekven and Uelen) should be opened.

The dated event is whale skulls at settlements, and the review itself reports the objection that whale remains alone do not prove hunting; a dated find of whaling harpoon heads (the review mentions them at the Okvik site without a date) would be firmer.
The US National Park Service page for Cape Krusenstern gives the Old Whaling culture as around 1,800 BCE, which differs from the 1200-800 BCE radiocarbon range in the review.
The review says most Old Bering Sea whale remains are gray whales, so when bowhead whaling in particular began (Punuk and Thule periods) needs a dated source.
The Bangudae petroglyphs in Korea and the Un'en'en carving in Chukotka were not checked for earlier North Pacific whaling, and Basque whaling was not checked.

research.note: The review does not say whether Bering Strait whaling arose with or without knowledge of whaling elsewhere in the North Pacific, and earlier claims there (Korea, Chukotka) were not checked.
